analysis.one_liner: Requires stronger vetting and borrower protections in federal student loan servicing contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 with four Democratic senators behind it, referred to the Senate education committee, and never advanced before the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Education Department to screen student loan servicers on their past performance, error rates, and treatment of borrowers before handing them federal contracts. It would require servicers to suspend interest during errors they caused, refund overpayments and fees, count missed forgiveness credit toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment, fix credit reports damaged by servicer mistakes, keep borrower records, and make borrower information available in multiple languages. It would also let the Department revoke contracts from servicers that misled it during vetting, and order a government study of how loan transfers between servicers hurt borrowers' credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers — roughly 40 million people whose loans are serviced by private companies under Education Department contracts. Borrowers harmed by servicer errors would get interest-free forbearance while the error is fixed, refunds of overpayments and overdraft fees, credit toward loan forgiveness for time lost to errors, and deletion of wrongful negative credit entries. Non-English speakers and borrowers with disabilities would get forms and services in their language or format.

how_it_helps.text: Before awarding a servicing contract, the Education Secretary must evaluate a servicer's track record: consumer satisfaction, error and disruption rates, past penalties, legal actions against it, and its ability to serve at-risk borrowers, non-English speakers, and borrowers with disabilities.

Servicers must place a borrower into interest-free administrative forbearance while they fix their own error, and the time lost counts toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment plans.
Servicers must refund overpayments caused by their errors, reimburse fees like insufficient-funds charges, and have credit bureaus delete delinquencies the servicer caused.

Servicers must keep borrower account records during servicing and for at least three years afterward, and the Education Secretary can revoke the contract of a servicer that misled the Department during vetting.
The Government Accountability Office would study how transferring loans between servicers disrupts repayment and damages credit scores, and recommend fixes.

analysis.who_pays: Federal student loan servicing companies — including firms like Nelnet, MOHELA, and Edfinancial — would face vetting scrutiny, new mandatory contract terms, refund and reimbursement obligations, recordkeeping requirements, and the possibility of losing their contracts. Some added compliance costs could flow back to the government through contract pricing, meaning taxpayers share some of the burden.

drawbacks.text: The new protections apply only to contracts signed at least 90 days after enactment; existing 'legacy' contracts would get a review but not the new mandatory terms, so borrowers under current contracts would not immediately gain these rights.

The bill gives the Education Department sole discretion over vetting, remedies, and contract revocation, with only notice and a hearing required before revocation — its effectiveness depends entirely on the Department enforcing its own contracts, and there is no private right of action for borrowers.
The refund, forbearance, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements would raise servicers' costs of doing business, which could translate into higher contract prices paid by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The borrower protections are concrete and targeted at a real, documented harm — servicer errors that cost borrowers money, time toward forgiveness, and credit standing. The costs are modest and mostly borne by servicing companies, with some pass-through to taxpayers. The main design weakness is that it applies mainly to future contracts and leans entirely on the Education Department's own enforcement, which is the same agency that allowed the problems to persist. On balance the benefits to borrowers outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate's education committee from June 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025; the committee never voted on it and the Senate never considered it.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, joined by Senators Klobuchar, Van Hollen, and Padilla.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan servicing companies are better off: no new vetting, refund, forbearance, or recordkeeping obligations ever took effect, and no servicer faced the possibility of contract revocation. Borrowers with servicer-caused errors gained nothing.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and the committee referral path it followed.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 5, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; there is no record of Republican opposition because the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.note: Companies servicing federal student loans under Education Department contracts would face pre-contract vetting of their error records, mandatory interest-free forbearance and refunds when they err, credit-report corrections, recordkeeping duties, and possible contract revocation for misleading the Department. These protections exist because servicer errors cost borrowers money, forgiveness credit, and credit standing.

Servicers would be required to have delinquencies caused by servicer errors removed from borrowers' credit reports, requiring bureaus to process corrections they do not currently receive as a matter of this contract structure. The effect on the bureaus' own revenue is small.
